title: When the Guard Adds Nothing: A Preregistered Paired Evaluation of Generate–Validate–Repair for LLM‑Produced Vendor CLI Configurations
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory experiment (n=300 paired tasks) that measured whether a deterministic generate–validate–repair (G‑V‑R) pipeline increases the probability that an LLM‑produced vendor CLI configuration passes a conservative deterministic validator, compared to direct LLM generation. The preregistration froze a single shared initial candidate per task and permitted at most one automatic repair call in the guarded arm when that initial candidate failed. Under the declared generator snapshot (gpt‑5‑mini) and prompt, every shared initial candidate passed the deterministic validator: baseline = 300/300; guarded = 300/300. The preregistered paired test yields n11 = 300, n10 = n01 = n00 = 0; paired difference = 0.00; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.00; paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI = [0.00, 0.00] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). Because no initial failures occurred, the preregistered single‑repair policy was not invoked. All execution artifacts, per‑episode validator traces, provider call traces, and analysis inputs/outputs are archived and hash‑signed to enable exact reproduction (see Disclosure). We analyze implications for when bounded automatic repairs are likely to help, describe concrete follow‑ups, and provide the full artifact pointers used in our reconciled confirmatory analysis.

sections.introduction: Generative natural‑language‑to‑configuration systems aim to reduce operator effort in NetOps by translating operator intent into vendor CLI changes. A common safety architecture is generate–validate–repair (G‑V‑R): a generator produces candidate CLI fragments, a deterministic validator enforces syntactic and workflow invariants, and an automatic repair stage attempts bounded corrections when validation fails. Prior literature explores many variants—tool‑assisted self‑refinement, verifier‑guided generation, and multi‑agent orchestration—but empirical guidance on when a bounded automatic repair stage provides measurable benefit in production‑like NetOps tasks is limited. We designed a confirmatory, preregistered paired experiment to isolate the marginal effect of a single automatic repair on a fixed candidate by sharing the same initial generator output across both arms (baseline vs guarded). The primary research question (preregistered) is: To what extent does a deterministic G‑V‑R pipeline increase the proportion of validator‑passing vendor configurations produced from operator intent, compared with direct LLM generation, when the two arms share the same initial candidate per task?
sections.related_work: Intent‑to‑configuration and intent‑driven NetOps have seen active recent work (intent translation systems and intent‑guided agents; e.g., Nguyen et al., 2024; Chakraborty et al., 2024; Mondal et al., 2025). Deterministic verification methods and SMT‑based approaches for network policy verification (Bagpipe / Weitz et al., 2016) are canonical references for validator construction; tool‑augmented self‑refinement work (INTERACSPARQL; Jian et al., 2026) and bounded lookahead/repair approaches (LATCH; Li et al., 2026) motivate constrained‑repair policies. We intentionally cite primary, verifiable sources and anchor our experiment design to conservative deterministic validation practices (parser + workflow invariants) rather than softer human‑preference judging. The reader may consult the artifact bundle for the exact manifest and validator implementation referenced below (artifact SHAs appear in the Disclosure).
sections.methodology: Preregistration. The full machine‑readable preregistration (study_hosted_netops_gvr_v1_cnd_7a3f2b1e) froze the design, estimands, inclusion/exclusion rules, retry/missingness policy, and analysis plan prior to execution (SHA‑256 = a85d66d4c6ce2275e2d8c820f96c610532dbb5452bebb3fe108848f9dc38cdf6). Design summary. Paired design (n = 300 tasks): for each task the pipeline produced a single shared initial candidate (one model call). Baseline outcome = validator(initial). Guarded outcome = validator(initial) or, if initial failed, invoke at most one automatic repair call and re‑validate; guarded success if repaired candidate passes. This shared‑initial design isolates the contribution of the repair step for a fixed initial proposal and bounds model‑call budget (baseline ≤1 call; guarded ≤2 calls). Task manifest and validator. We used a curated 300‑task multi‑vendor manifest restricted to vendor CLI fragments expressing configuration‑change intents with explicit ordering/safety constraints and expected final states. Canonical manifest path: execution/task_manifest.jsonl (SHA‑256 = 6d99060659a722e6a91dd2abd7baca45a2aefb41e124b049124d5ea2632cb4b3). The deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5, version 5.0) enforces parsing, canonicalization, syntactic correctness, interface assignment invariants, make‑before‑break and down‑before‑change patterns when required, and destructive‑pattern detection. Execution contract and model snapshot. The adapter family hosted_netops_gvr_v1 executed the preregistered contract in scientific_confirmatory mode using the declared generator snapshot gpt‑5‑mini (execution/model_configuration.json; SHA‑256 = 1acce92558edeb13cd97b75817329d332afe4a36d01d566f1a26c61b132923fa). Stopping and missingness. The preregistered stopping rule required running all 300 pairs once; technical retries for transient provider failures were recorded; failed calls were handled according to the preregistered missingness plan. Analysis plan. The primary estimand was the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline. The preregistered primary test was an exact McNemar two‑sided test on paired binary outcomes; we also compute a paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) as specified in the preregistration.
sections.results: Execution bookkeeping. The run completed exactly as preregistered: planned episodes = 600, completed episodes = 600, failed episodes = 0; model_calls_used = 300 (one shared initial generation per task); maximum_model_calls allowed = 600. Relevant artifact paths and SHA‑256s are reported in the Disclosure. Confirmatory outcomes (artifact‑grounded). Every shared initial candidate passed the deterministic validator without invoking automatic repair: baseline_success_count = 300/300; guarded_success_count = 300/300. The paired contingency table (guarded × baseline) is n11 = 300, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0 (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv; SHA‑256 = a39fd3386c945cae095f2f310ead1f21ac600f8b2492bcd49b664c8da5782aa0). Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.00. Paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI = [0.00, 0.00] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). Repair activity. Because initial failure did not occur for any task, the preregistered guarded repair stage was never invoked (repair calls performed = 0). Representative episode examples. Per‑episode validator traces and canonicalized configurations are archived: e.g., execution/scoring/task-000001-baseline.json (SHA‑256 = 1c3cbbeb30cb9d0...), execution/responses/task-000001-shared-initial.txt (SHA‑256 = 8f38c8becd7e1e36...), and execution/provider_calls/task-000001-shared-initial.json (SHA‑256 = a59191a39575bd60...). These artifacts record the exact strings, normalized canonicalizations, validator diagnostic fields (violation codes, parsed command counts), and hashes used in analysis.
sections.discussion: Interpretation of the null observed effect. The preregistered paired test was designed to detect an improvement in validator passes due to a bounded automatic repair when initial candidates sometimes fail. In this run the generator+prompt+snapshot combination produced validator‑passing shared initial candidates for every task, producing a ceiling outcome and zero discordant pairs. Statistically, this yields a paired difference of 0.00, McNemar p = 1.00, and a degenerate bootstrap CI [0.00,0.00]. This outcome is an artifact‑grounded factual observation about the chosen generator snapshot, prompt, and curated task distribution; it is not evidence that repair is never useful in other regimes. Why the shared‑initial design? We preregistered a shared‑initial design to isolate repair marginality for a fixed proposed candidate and to bound model‑call budgets. That design increases internal clarity at the cost of sensitivity to ceiling effects when the generator is already highly accurate on the task set. Reviewer‑requested per‑vendor analyses. The preregistration specified per‑vendor secondary paired tests (Cisco IOS, JunOS, Arista). We did not present separate per‑vendor statistics because no discordant pairs occurred overall and therefore within every vendor subgroup; per‑vendor McNemar tests are not informative when discordance is zero. The canonical task_manifest.jsonl (execution/task_manifest.jsonl; SHA‑256 = 6d99060659a722e6a91dd2abd7baca45a2aefb41e124b049124d5ea2632cb4b3) contains vendor labels and enables auditors to compute subgroup counts programmatically; our conclusion about per‑vendor inconsequence follows deterministically from the paired contingency table (n11=300, n10=n01=n00=0) and the manifest. Operational implications. Practically, when a given generator/prompt produces validator‑passing candidates on the operational task set, adding a bounded automatic repair stage does not increase deterministic pass rates but does add cost and system complexity. However, a bounded repair may still be valuable in other regimes: (1) under harder/adversarial tasks, (2) if the generator is weaker or different snapshots are used, (3) for independent initial draws per arm (no shared initial), or (4) when repair budgets permit multiple iterative repairs. We provide the archived artifacts to support exact replay and controlled perturbation experiments to explore these regimes.
sections.conclusion: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory experiment to measure whether a bounded G‑V‑R pipeline improves deterministic validator pass rates over direct LLM generation for vendor CLI fragments. For the chosen prompt and the declared generator snapshot (gpt‑5‑mini), every shared initial candidate (n=300) passed the conservative deterministic validator; consequently, the preregistered single‑repair policy was never invoked and produced no measurable benefit (paired difference = 0.00; McNemar p = 1.00; bootstrap 95% CI = [0.00, 0.00]). This narrow, artifact‑grounded result highlights that the incremental value of bounded automatic repair depends critically on the generator/prompt/task regime and that preregistered designs that share initial candidates are especially informative about marginal repair value but susceptible to ceiling effects. All raw outputs, provider traces, validator traces, and analysis inputs/outputs are archived and hash‑signed to enable exact reproduction and targeted follow‑ups that vary task hardness, prompt engineering, model snapshot, or repair budget (artifact pointers below and in the Disclosure).

limitations: Single generator snapshot (gpt-5-mini) evaluated — results do not generalize to other models or prompt variants.

Deterministic validator implements a conservative subset of operational checks (parsing, canonicalization, workflow invariants) and omits deeper dynamic/emulation‑level checks and full inter‑router routing semantics.

Curated 300‑task manifest may not include adversarial or out‑of‑distribution failure modes; for the declared prompt and model snapshot every shared initial candidate passed the validator (ceiling effect), limiting the ability to measure G‑V‑R improvements under the preregistered one‑repair policy.
Shared initial‑candidate design (preregistered) isolates repair marginality for a fixed proposal but reduces sensitivity when the generator is already accurate on the manifest.
Only a single automatic repair attempt was permitted per task; iterative or human‑in‑the‑loop repair policies were not evaluated.
Automated contamination detection reduces but cannot entirely exclude memorization risk; residual uncertainty remains despite no flagged pairs.
